You're wrong. The law already has several Safe Harbor exemptions which hold content hosts unaccountable for illegal content as long as they make a good faith effort to report said content to authorities and cooperate in any investigations, and as long as they take a "neutral and organic stance to content curation" (Basically, they just moderate content that violates the rules, and don't take political sides). In short, because the Admins take a neutral stance and let Users organically curate content within the rules and cut out content that is reported to them that violates the rules, as well as report illegal content they discover to the authorities, they are then assumed not to personally endorse illegal content that shows up. If they take steps to personally curate content in a biased and directed manner, though, because they are removing content they personally disagree with, then anything that remains is therefore, legally, something that can be assumed to be endorsed. Ironically enough, by artificially curating content on their servers, such as taking Admin action to hide the posts critical of the migrants in Germany and conservative news posts here in the USA, Facebook has surrendered the Safe Harbor exemptions they took for granted, because by personally taking Admin action to curate certain types of content they want to show up, they have opened themselves up to the accusation that any content they did not remove is content they approve of, including any illicit content they did not report to authorities.

In short, what FB, Reddit, and the like, have done by going after all of this "Hate Speech" and "Harrassment" that is really anything but, has been to eliminate their own legal protections, under the law, by voluntarily surrendering their own Safe Harbor exemptions. This lawsuit has been a long time coming, and it's about time FB and the rest of these Silicon Valley companies return to understanding why a "Free Speech" stance and neutral admin stance on content curation was important in the first place.

The DMCA also has similar Safe Harbor provisions, though being something covering civil litigation, the provisions are a bit different. But the basic spirit behind them are still the same. Good faith compliance with the Law, and political/ideological neutrality of curation of content shields the provider from litigation (Civil or Criminal), assuming certain benchmarks of behavior are met.

That being said, I am quite confident that Facebook, Twitter, and Reddit all gave up their Safe Harbor exemptions when they began policing speech and political discussion they were ideologically opposed to, both in letter of the law and spirit. And I say it's about time they are reminded why said neutral curation stance was so important, in the first place.
